title: In defense of Asian American art
gist: Noah Smith argues that the category 'Asian American art' is defined too narrowly (art both by AND about Asian Americans), which confines it to a small, repetitive, transient micro-genre destined to shrink as assimilation accelerates; he advocates counting any work by Asian American creators, citing a wide catalog of graphic novels, TV, music, and sci-fi that break the standard format.

insights.claim: Media only gets labeled 'Asian American' when it is both made by Asian Americans AND about Asian American culture, a double criterion that confines the category to a narrow slice and excludes most work by Asian American creators.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A demand-side reframing: broadening a cultural category expands the addressable creator pool and content library, relevant to how streamers and publishers segment and market diverse IP.
insights.quote: movies, TV shows, books, etc. only get labeled “Asian American” if they satisfy both of these criteria at once. But that’s a pretty narrow slice of art!
insights.locator: “Asian American art” is defined too narrowly

insights.claim: The 2010s identity-politics norm that authors should only write about groups they belong to suppresses cross-over stories about Asian Americans by non-Asian creators, shrinking the volume of such narratives that get told.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
entities: Harold & Kumar Go to White Castle
insights.so_what: Cultural gatekeeping norms constrain the supply of marketable stories; a loosening of those norms would widen the creative funnel for studios.
insights.quote: the culture of the 2010s really put a damper on that sort of crossover
insights.locator: First, it excludes art made about Asian Americans by non-Asians

insights.claim: Avatar: The Last Airbender drew heavily on Chinese, Japanese, Tibetan, and Korean cultures in a distinctly American style but is not counted as Asian American art because its creators were white, illustrating how the by-and-about definition mislabels culturally Asian-influenced work.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: IP value and cultural attribution can diverge; ATLA is framed as the best US fantasy IP since ~2000, a franchise-scale asset whose lineage is under-recognized.
insights.quote: arguably the best new fantasy IP to come out of the U.S. since the turn of the century
insights.locator: The clearest example of this is Avatar: the Last Airbender

insights.claim: Excluding South Asians, Asian Americans are only about 5.5% of the U.S. population, making the standard 'Asian American culture' subject matter a small pool of source material for storytelling.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A small, narrowly-defined audience segment caps the commercial scale of format-bound 'Asian American' content, favoring genre-agnostic creator strategies.
insights.quote: Asian Americans are only around 5.5% of the U.S. population
insights.locator: It’s not that big, for one thing

insights.claim: Around two-thirds of Asian Americans report having close friends of another race and over 40% of U.S.-born Asian Americans marry outside their race, evidence that Asian Americans are assimilating faster than the white European immigrants of a century ago.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Rapid assimilation erodes both the source material and the natural audience for immigrant-narrative content, implying the genre's addressable market is structurally declining.
insights.quote: over 40% of U.S.-born Asian Americans marry people of other races
insights.locator: Around two-thirds of Asian Americans report having close friends

insights.claim: The classic second-generation immigrant experience rarely persists past the second generation, so the source material and natural audience for 'Asian American' narratives as currently defined are destined to shrink into a transitory micro-genre.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Content built on a generational-immigrant premise has a limited shelf life; long-term value accrues to creators who move beyond the format.
insights.quote: both the source material and the natural audience for what we now consider “Asian American” narratives are destined to shrink

insights.claim: A large body of high-quality work by Asian American creators sits outside the standard format, spanning graphic novels (Adrian Tomine's Shortcomings, adapted to film in 2023; Marjorie Liu and Sana Takeda's Monstress), TV (Lee Sung Jin's BEEF), music (Michelle Zauner's Japanese Breakfast; Natalie Lu's Wisp), and science fiction (Yoon Ha Lee, Ted Chiang, Fonda Lee, Charles Yu).
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The real creative supply from this cohort is far larger than the marketed 'Asian American' slate, signaling an under-tapped talent pipeline for publishers and studios.
insights.locator: A few examples of great Asian American art

insights.claim: Asian American creators increasingly contribute to non-Asian productions, exemplified by Hiro Murai, who Donald Glover said 'had the eye for' the all-Black-written series Atlanta, directing the pilot and many episodes plus Childish Gambino's 'This Is America' video.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Creative value from a cohort shows up diffusely across projects it doesn't nominally 'represent,' so category-based talent scouting understates its reach.
insights.quote: had the eye for this show

insights.claim: A short film by 19-year-old Wesley Wang, 'Nothing, Except Everything,' drew a feature-film directing deal from Darren Aronofsky after he saw it, an example of low-budget breakout work converting directly into a studio commitment.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Illustrates the talent-discovery path where viral short work leads to feature deals, a scouting signal for emerging creators.
insights.quote: he immediately called Wang up and gave him a deal to direct a feature film
insights.locator: 11. Nothing, Except Everything, by Wesley Wang

insights.claim: Because writing graphic novels takes enormous time for little money, a creator with a hit is financially forced to keep it running as long as possible, causing long-running series to meander; the fix is for TV producers to adapt graphic novels early in their runs.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The economics of serialized comics create a quality-decay incentive, pointing to early TV adaptation as the value-capture path for both creators and studios.
insights.quote: once a graphic novelist gets a hit, they are financially forced to keep it running for as long as possible

insights.claim: The commercial, if modest, success of format-standard 'Asian American' works like The Joy Luck Club and Crazy Rich Asians opened doors for Asian American creators to enter entertainment and gain freedom to make work about any subject.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Early-genre hits function as market-access infrastructure for a creator cohort, so their downstream option value exceeds their direct box office.
insights.quote: its often modest success opened the door for a lot of Asian American creators to break into the worlds of art and entertainment
insights.locator: And to the snarky people on X
